title: Researchers Report Subsurface Anomalies at Turkey's Durupinar Site
excerpt: Researchers report unusual soil samples and underground patterns at Turkey's Durupinar formation, but laboratory results have yet to establish a link to Noah's Ark.
content:
Unusual underground patterns and soil characteristics at Turkey's Durupinar formation have prompted renewed claims that the site could be connected to Noah's Ark, according to the American research group Noah's Ark Scans. The team has collected soil samples and conducted subsurface surveys near Mount Ararat, but laboratory analysis remains necessary to determine what the findings represent.

The formation measures approximately 515 to 538 feet long, according to Noah's Ark Scans, whose researchers argue that its boat-like outline resembles the biblical vessel described in Genesis. The site lies about 18 miles from Mount Ararat and approximately 6,500 feet above sea level.

Geologists have previously argued that the formation is a natural landform. A 1996 paper co-authored by Lorence Gene Collins, a geologist at California State University, Northridge, concluded that it was a completely natural rock formation, according to a fact-checking report published by Yahoo.

Andrew Jones, founder of Noah's Ark Scans, said a 2024 soil study identified differences between the formation and the surrounding hillside.

"The studies showed that there is three times more organic matter inside the boat-shaped area than immediately outside it," Jones said.

Jones also described differences in the composition of the surrounding ground, which researchers intend to investigate through further laboratory testing.

"The soil within the formation is different from the soil on the mountainside."

The research team conducted its first core-drilling campaign, reaching a depth of 18 meters at one location and drilling between 5 and 8 meters at several others. More than 300 samples were collected and sent to Ankara University laboratories for analysis, Jones said.

The samples will be examined for possible evidence of decayed wood, animal remains and human activity. Researchers also reported finding substantial deposits of dark soil during drilling, but those observations have not established that the formation contains remains of an ancient vessel.

Jones said the team's drilling results challenged the suggestion that the entire formation consists of solid bedrock.

"They've criticized in the past, saying all those scans you can interpret different ways, 'This is a solid mass of rock, a syncline or a block of bedrock,'" Jones said.

He said drilling at more than 12 locations had not revealed the solid rock layer that critics had suggested was present. The team plans additional testing to establish the composition of the soil.

"Noah's Ark was a giant wooden boat, according to the Bible," Jones said.

Jones said the researchers hoped laboratory analysis would clarify whether the organic material found in the formation could be explained by decaying wood or other processes. No confirmed identification of wooden structural remains has been reported in the supplied research accounts.

Dr. Khosrow Bakhtar, a former Department of Defense researcher, used his subsurface scanning technology, known as BakhtarRadar, to examine the site. He said the scans revealed organized patterns, possible underground corridors and voids at different depths.

Bakhtar described the results as unusual compared with his previous professional experience.

"This is the most significant finding for 40 years of my career. I have never seen this kind of anomaly before," Bakhtar said.

According to Jones, some suspected underground voids appear to be 3 to 4 meters below the surface, while others extend to approximately 13 meters. The researchers have also described right-angle patterns and layered structures that they believe warrant further investigation.

Bakhtar said the repeated patterns appeared to be associated with one underlying object, although he did not identify what produced them.

"If the anomalies were not important, we would not have seen them at all," Bakhtar said.

He said the apparent alignment of the patterns influenced his interpretation of the scans, while acknowledging uncertainty about the object's identity.

"I am a hundred per cent sure that they come from the same original object."

In a separate development, a video circulating online that purported to show an excavation of Noah's Ark near Mount Ararat was identified as AI-generated by the fact-checking outlet Lead Stories. The OpenAI Verify tool detected a SynthID watermark, while Hive Moderation assessed the video as 99.9% likely to be AI-generated.

The video was posted by the @JohnmichealC1 account on X on October 5, 2026. The fact-checkers also noted that the location shown did not resemble the actual Durupinar formation.

Researchers have additionally pointed to 26 large carved stones with holes in a valley leading toward the formation, suggesting that they may have served as anchor weights. Marine fossils, shells and sand dollars found in the wider region have also been cited by supporters of the theory, although their presence does not independently establish a connection to the biblical flood.

"We still have the lab work to do," Jones said.
